tldr: Using a client-facing insurance RAG chatbot as the example, Pacquetet lays out an evaluation pipeline built on a written evaluation dataset, narrow pass/fail metrics and human-calibrated LLM judges.
summary: Pacquetet, a senior AI scientist at SCIAM, argues that the gap between an AI demo and production is trust, and that trust comes from turning 'try a question and eyeball it' into a pipeline that outputs a score at the click of a button, used before each release and to guide every prompt or architecture change. The pipeline has three steps: simulate inputs across ideal, realistic (typos, keywords, a vague 'am I covered?') and adversarial (prompt injection, jailbreaks) scenarios; run them through the system; evaluate the outputs. Latency, cost and stability are monitored as for any service.

Her example chatbot has a triage agent that outputs only true or false, scored by simple string matching, followed by a RAG agent that writes the answer. The hard part is that free text. Working through 'Is renter's insurance mandatory for a tenant in France?', she shows correctness, relevance, completeness and safety pulling against business rules like a warm tone and short answers, with several different answers all acceptable. Writing expected answers in the evaluation dataset is slow, but it turns vague specs such as 'short' into a concrete contract with the business team.

She ranks metrics from deterministic (regex, string matching, F1) through similarity metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore) to LLM-as-a-judge and human review. A judge works when given one narrow task, such as 'return true if the new answer contradicts the expected one', never 'is this answer good?'. Each question combines several pass/fail checks, secondary metrics such as a follow-up question are tracked without gating, and the judges are calibrated against business reviewers until verdicts agree. The continuous drift monitoring promised in the abstract was not covered.
keyPoints: Test inputs should cover three scenarios: ideal, realistic and adversarial; teams often skip the realistic one.
The evaluation dataset of inputs and expected outputs works as the executable spec and exposes contradictory or implicit business rules.
Prefer deterministic metrics whenever possible; semantic similarity cannot detect a wrong fact or a bad tone.
An LLM judge is reliable only with a narrow binary task, such as detecting contradictions with the reference answer.

Combine per-question pass/fail checks (a contradiction judge plus string matching for a required phone number), keep secondary metrics like a follow-up question non-blocking, and calibrate everything against human reviewers.
takeaways: Write expected answers for a set of ideal, realistic and adversarial questions together with your business team before tuning prompts.
Use string matching or regex for anything constrained, and keep LLM judges for the parts that need comprehension.
Rewrite any 'is this answer good?' judge prompt into single-purpose true/false checks.
Have business reviewers score a sample of outputs and adjust your judges until their verdicts match.

quotes.text: If you want to find balance, you have to give up control.

watchIf: You have an LLM or RAG prototype that works in demos and need a defensible way to show it is good enough for real users.
